fields.definition: On the ngoni, a small West African (Mande) plucked lute with a hide-covered wooden body and gut or nylon strings, a plucked note that sounds with a short, tight, quickly decaying tone having little sustain or ringing resonance, giving a dry, percussive character.
fields.plain_english: The ngoni is a small West African lute with a skin-covered body. A dry pluck is a plucked note that stops ringing fast. It sounds short and snappy, not long and echoey.
fields.purpose_function: The dry, fast-decaying pluck gives the ngoni its crisp rhythmic drive, letting fast melodic runs stay clear and articulate without notes blurring into one another.
fields.practical_application: An engineer captures the ngoni close with a small-diaphragm condenser to preserve its tight transient, avoiding excess room sound that would smear the naturally dry, percussive notes.
common_mistakes: Confusing the ngoni with the kora; the kora is a large 21-string harp-lute with long sustain, while the ngoni is small with a short, dry decay
Drenching the ngoni in reverb, which masks its tight, percussive attack
Treating a dry pluck as a technical fault, when it is the instrument's natural short-sustain voice
scenario_contexts: Miking a ngoni for a Mande griot recording where rhythmic clarity matters
Blending ngoni with kora and balafon in a West African ensemble mix
Choosing close mic placement to preserve the ngoni's dry, articulate transient

sources: Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, Vol. 1: Africa

fields.definition: On the nyckelharpa, a bowed Swedish keyed fiddle fitted with a set of undertuned sympathetic strings, the bright, ringing, halo-like resonance produced when those sympathetic strings vibrate in sympathy with the bowed melody notes, adding a shimmering, reverb-like sheen to the tone.
fields.plain_english: A nyckelharpa is a Swedish fiddle played with a bow and rows of keys. Under the main strings sit extra strings that no one bows. They ring on their own when you play, adding a bright, shimmery glow like a soft echo.
fields.purpose_function: The sympathetic-string shimmer enriches the nyckelharpa's tone with a natural, sustained resonance, giving it a characteristic bright, ringing sustain even on short bow strokes.
fields.practical_application: An engineer recording nyckelharpa avoids over-close mic placement and heavy upper-mid EQ cuts so the delicate sympathetic shimmer stays audible, often adding a little room capture to let it bloom.
common_mistakes: Confusing the sympathetic strings, which are never bowed, with the melody strings the bow and keys play
Cutting high-mid frequencies so hard in the mix that the shimmer disappears
Damping the body or using too many close mics, which chokes the ringing resonance
scenario_contexts: Recording a solo nyckelharpa where the sympathetic shimmer is central to the sound
Placing a room mic to capture the halo of resonance around the direct tone
Blending nyckelharpa into a Nordic folk mix without masking its ringing overtones

sources: Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, Vol. 8: Europe

fields.definition: The incidental squeaks, scrapes, and thumps produced when a player's fingers slide along or release the strings of a nylon-string (classical) guitar, most audible on the metal-wound bass strings where the fingertips drag across the winding while shifting position.
fields.plain_english: On a classical guitar, the low strings are wrapped in thin metal. When a player slides their fingers along them to change notes, the fingers catch the ridges and squeak. That squeak is finger noise.
fields.purpose_function: Finger noise is a natural by-product of moving the fingers on the strings; in a recording it can lend intimate realism, but at high levels it distracts from the notes and must be managed.
fields.practical_application: When recording classical guitar, an engineer manages finger squeak through mic choice and placement, gentle high-frequency EQ, or careful editing, and may advise the player on smoother shifts or coated strings.
common_mistakes: Trying to erase every squeak, which strips natural realism and sounds artificial
Blaming the guitar, when smoother left-hand position shifts reduce the noise more than gear changes
Assuming the plain treble nylon strings squeak, when the noise comes mostly from the metal-wound bass strings
scenario_contexts: Editing squeaks out of a solo classical guitar take before mastering
Choosing a mic position that reduces finger noise on a close-miked nylon guitar
Advising a guitarist on coated strings or cleaner shifts to cut down squeak

fields.definition: The full, freely sustaining tone produced when a string is played open, sounded along its entire length without being stopped by a finger or fret, allowing it to vibrate and ring longer and more resonantly than a fretted note and to resonate sympathetically with related pitches.
fields.plain_english: An open string is one you play without pressing it down. With nothing stopping it, the whole string is free to vibrate. So it rings out longer and louder than a note you hold down with a finger.
fields.purpose_function: Open-string ring gives players sustained, resonant tones and lets a note keep sounding while the hand moves elsewhere; it also adds sympathetic resonance that enriches an instrument's overall sound.
fields.practical_application: Guitarists and engineers use open-string ring for drones, arpeggios, and sustain, but watch for unwanted ringing bleeding into later notes, muting strings by hand when a cleaner, drier passage is needed.
common_mistakes: Letting open strings ring into a passage where they clash with the harmony, muddying the chord
Forgetting to mute a ringing open string before it bleeds into the next section
Assuming a fretted note rings as long as an open string, when open strings usually sustain longer
scenario_contexts: Using open strings as a drone under a fingerpicked guitar part
Muting ringing open strings to keep a tight, dry rhythm part clean
Tuning a mix so sympathetic open-string resonance supports rather than clutters the track

sources: Grove Dictionary of Musical Instruments (open string)
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments

fields.definition: On the Japanese koto and related zithers, a left-hand technique in which the player presses down on a string on the far side of its movable bridge, increasing tension to raise the pitch, typically by a semitone or whole tone, allowing pitch bends and ornaments beyond the tuning fixed by the bridge positions.
fields.plain_english: A koto has movable bridges that set each string pitch. With oshide, the player presses the string down on one side of its bridge. That tightens the string, so the note bends up higher, like bending a guitar string.
fields.purpose_function: Oshide lets the koto reach pitches and expressive bends the fixed bridge tuning cannot provide, adding vibrato, ornaments, and note-to-note pitch slides central to the instrument's musical style.
fields.practical_application: A player uses oshide to raise a plucked note or add an ornament; a recording engineer captures it with enough dynamic range and low-noise gain to preserve the subtle pitch rise and the string's changing tension.
common_mistakes: Pressing so hard the pitch overshoots the intended semitone or whole tone
Confusing oshide, pressing left of the bridge to raise pitch, with moving the bridge itself to retune
Pressing on the wrong side of the bridge, which slackens rather than tightens the string
scenario_contexts: Performing a koto ornament that bends a plucked note up a semitone
Recording traditional koto where oshide pitch slides must stay clearly audible
Notating oshide press-bends in a transcription of Japanese zither music

sources: Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, Vol. 7: East Asia

fields.definition: On the pedal steel guitar, the smooth pitch changes produced two ways: sliding the handheld steel bar along the strings for continuous glides (portamento), and pressing foot pedals or knee levers that mechanically alter the tension of chosen strings through the changer to bend individual notes up or down while other notes sustain.
fields.plain_english: A pedal steel is played flat, sliding a metal bar over the strings. Moving the bar slides the pitch up or down smoothly. Foot pedals and knee levers can also bend single strings while the rest hold, giving that crying, gliding country sound.
fields.purpose_function: Bends and glides give the pedal steel its vocal, weeping character and let a player bend some notes within a chord while others stay put, creating the smooth voice-leading that defines the instrument.
fields.practical_application: A player combines bar glides with pedal and knee-lever bends for expressive lines; an engineer records the instrument with a clean, full-range signal so the sustained, gliding pitches and their overtones come through without distortion.
common_mistakes: Confusing bar glides, made by moving the steel, with pedal or knee-lever bends, made by mechanical string-tension changes
Assuming all strings bend together, when pedals and levers bend only the strings they are set to
Sliding the bar carelessly so glides land off-pitch instead of on the target note
scenario_contexts: Recording a country ballad where pedal-steel glides answer the vocal line
Setting up a pedal steel's copedent so specific strings bend on each pedal
Blending a pedal steel's sustained bends into a mix without masking the lead vocal

sources: Grove Dictionary of Musical Instruments (steel guitar / pedal steel guitar)

fields.definition: On the pipa, a Chinese four-string fretted lute plucked with the fingernails, a sharp, percussive plucking attack in which a string is struck or pulled and released hard so it produces a bright, biting snap, sometimes rebounding against the frets, adding crisp accent and attack.
fields.plain_english: The pipa is a Chinese lute plucked with the fingernails. A snap is a hard, sharp pluck. The string is hit or pulled and let go so it cracks out a bright, punchy sound, a bit like a slapped bass note.
fields.purpose_function: The snap gives the pipa strong rhythmic accents and a percussive edge, cutting through an ensemble and marking beats or dramatic moments with a sharp, attacking transient.
fields.practical_application: An engineer recording pipa leaves enough headroom for the snap's fast, loud transient so it stays punchy and undistorted, and may use gentle compression to keep snaps even without dulling their attack.
common_mistakes: Setting record levels too hot so the snap's sharp transient clips and distorts
Over-compressing until the snap loses its percussive attack
Confusing the percussive snap with the smooth sweeping strum (sao)
scenario_contexts: Capturing a pipa solo where sharp snaps punctuate the melody
Leaving headroom on the pipa channel for loud snapped accents
Balancing snapped accents against sustained tremolo passages in a mix

sources: Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, Vol. 7: East Asia (China)

fields.definition: On the pipa, the technique called sao, a rapid outward strum in which the fingers sweep across all four strings almost at once, sounding them together in a strong, broad, slightly percussive rush of sound; its reverse-direction counterpart is fu.
fields.plain_english: On the pipa, sao means quickly brushing your fingers across all four strings at once. It is like a fast strum on a guitar. All the strings sound together in one broad, sweeping burst.
fields.purpose_function: Sao lets the pipa sound full chords and strong accents in a single sweep, adding power, fullness, and rhythmic drive that a single plucked string cannot provide.
fields.practical_application: A recording engineer captures sao sweeps with even coverage of all four strings and enough headroom for their combined loud transient, positioning the mic so the sweep sounds balanced rather than favoring one string.
common_mistakes: Confusing sao, a sweeping strum across all strings, with plucking one string at a time
Micing so close to one string that the sweep sounds uneven across the four strings
Reversing sao and fu, when sao sweeps outward and fu sweeps back in the opposite direction
scenario_contexts: Recording a dramatic pipa passage built on strong sao sweeps
Placing a mic to capture all four strings evenly during strummed sweeps
Balancing loud sao chords against quieter single-note lines in a mix

sources: Garland Encyclopedia of World Music, Vol. 7: East Asia (China)

fields.definition: The buzzing, rattling, or percussive timbre produced when an object such as a screw, bolt, coin, or piece of rubber is placed on or between a struck or plucked string, as on a prepared piano or prepared guitar, so the object vibrates loosely against the string and alters its normal pitched tone.
fields.plain_english: If you rest a small object like a screw on a piano or guitar string, the string rattles against it when played. Instead of a clear note, you get a buzzy, clattery sound. Composers like John Cage did this on purpose.
fields.purpose_function: Preparing a string with an added object turns a pitched instrument into a source of new percussive and noise-like colors, letting composers draw gong-like, buzzing, or drum-like sounds from a piano or guitar.
fields.practical_application: A player fixes objects to chosen strings following a preparation table, and an engineer mics the instrument closely to capture the delicate rattles and buzzes, watching levels so sudden loud rattles do not overload the input.
common_mistakes: Placing objects so loosely they fall off, or so tightly they fully mute the string instead of rattling
UNSAFE: forcing hard objects between piano strings or against the soundboard, which can damage the strings, bridge, or finish
Assuming any object gives the same sound, when material, size, and position each change the rattle
scenario_contexts: Recording a prepared-piano piece where each note has a different rattle
Following a composer's preparation chart to place objects on specific strings
Close-miking a prepared guitar to capture subtle string rattles

sources: Grove Dictionary of Musical Instruments (prepared piano)
